lines.text: Balloons, steam trains, Model Ts and jumbo jets. This is how people learned to travel faster and further, from the age of sail to the electric car.
It begins with two French paper makers, the Montgolfier brothers, who found that a bag of hot air could lift people into the sky.
In November 1783 their balloon carried people over Paris, the first free flight by humans and the start of the history of flight.
On the water, Robert Fulton's Clermont steamed up the Hudson River in 1807, the first steamboat to carry paying passengers as a business.
Ten years later Karl Drais built a running machine on two wheels. With pedals and a chain added later, the bicycle became cheap transport for millions.
In 1829 Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill Trials, and its design set the pattern for steam engines for a century.
A year later the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first line run wholly by steam, with timetables, passengers and freight.
Meanwhile inventors were building the first electric motors, the machines that would one day drive trains, and much later, cars.
Charles Goodyear found how to cure rubber with sulphur so it stayed firm in heat and cold, and the tyre became possible.
Karl Benz, a German engineer, would build a practical petrol car, and his wife Bertha would drive it a long way to prove it worked.
Otto Lilienthal flew gliders from hills near Berlin, thousands of flights that inspired the Wright brothers, before a crash took his life in 1896.
In 1859 Edwin Drake struck oil in Pennsylvania, setting off a boom and the start of the fuel that would power modern transport.
A year later Etienne Lenoir built a working engine that burned its fuel inside, the ancestor of every car, tractor and propeller plane.
In 1863 London opened the first underground railway in the world, and cities everywhere would follow it below ground.
Henry Ford would bring the moving assembly line to cars, and make them cheap enough for ordinary families.
Wilbur Wright, a bicycle maker from Ohio, worked out how to steer a wing using gliders and a wind tunnel.
In 1869 the American railroad reached the Pacific, cutting a journey of months down to about a week and opening the West.
That same year the Suez Canal opened across Egypt, shortening the sea route between Europe and Asia by thousands of kilometres.
Orville Wright, Wilbur's younger brother, would be at the controls for their first powered flight.
In 1886 Benz patented his Motorwagen, a three-wheeler with its own petrol engine, usually called the first practical car.
With it the automobile was born, a vehicle that would reshape cities, countries and daily life.
In 1893 Rudolf Diesel built an engine that lit its fuel by squeezing the air, and it still drives trucks, ships and trains.
Amelia Earhart would fly solo across the Atlantic in 1932, then vanish over the Pacific trying to circle the world.
Around 1900 Count von Zeppelin began his great airships, rigid giants that carried passengers before aeroplanes outclassed them.
Charles Lindbergh would fly alone and non-stop from New York to Paris, and become the most famous pilot in the world.
In 1903 Henry Ford founded his motor company, which would put a car within reach of ordinary families.
That same year the Trans-Siberian Railway opened, the longest line on Earth, linking Moscow with the Pacific coast of Russia.
And on a cold December day in 1903 at Kitty Hawk, the Wright Flyer lifted off, the first powered, controlled aeroplane flight.
Just four years later, in France, the first machines lifted by spinning rotors raised a person off the ground.
In 1908 William Durant gathered Buick, Oldsmobile and others into General Motors, for decades one of the largest car makers in the world.
The same year came the Ford Model T, simple and tough. Built on a moving line, more than fifteen million were sold.
In July 1909 Louis Bleriot flew his little monoplane across the English Channel, and many began to believe aeroplanes would matter.
In April 1912 the Titanic struck an iceberg on her first voyage and more than fifteen hundred died, leading to new rules on lifeboats and radio.
In 1914 the Panama Canal joined the Atlantic and Pacific, finished by the Americans after the French had failed, at a heavy cost in lives.
Route 66 opened in 1926 from Chicago to Los Angeles, and became the symbol of the open American road.
In May 1927 Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis across the Atlantic, alone and without stopping.
In 1935 the Douglas DC-3 made carrying passengers by air pay for the first time. Some are flying still.
The airship Hindenburg crossed the Atlantic in style, until it burst into flames while landing in New Jersey in 1937.
Britain's Spitfire, with its elegant curved wings, first flew in 1936 and helped defend the country in the Battle of Britain.
In the late thirties Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany each built the first jet engines.
In Japan a loom company spun off Toyota, whose way of building cars without waste would be copied around the world.
Germany's Volkswagen Beetle went on sale in 1938. Mass-produced after the war, more than twenty million were built.
In August 1939 the small Heinkel He 178 became the first aircraft to fly on a jet engine.
In the Second World War the Willys Jeep went wherever the Allies went, and later inspired a whole world of off-road cars.
Germany's Me 262 became the first jet fighter in combat, far faster than any propeller plane, but too late to change the war.
The American B-29, with its pressurised cabin, bombed Japan, and two of them dropped the atomic bombs in 1945.
After the war the rocket-powered Bell X-1 took Chuck Yeager past the speed of sound in 1947.
In Italy, Piaggio launched the Vespa scooter, cheap transport for postwar Europe and a symbol of Italian style.
In France the Citroen 2CV was built for farmers, soft enough to cross a ploughed field, and it stayed in production for more than forty years.
In America, Ford's F-Series pickup arrived in 1948, and became the country's best-selling vehicle for decades.
The Comet was the first jet airliner in service. Crashes traced to metal fatigue around its square windows taught the industry a hard lesson.
The B-52 bomber first flew in 1952 and, through endless upgrades, is still in service more than seventy years on.
Then in 1956 Malcolm McLean shipped goods in a standard steel box, and the humble container made world trade cheap.
The Boeing 707 made jet travel common from 1958, carrying passengers across oceans and making Boeing the leading maker of airliners.
Honda's Super Cub, light and easy to ride, became the best-selling motor vehicle of all time.
In 1959 Britain's Mini turned its engine sideways to leave room for people, and became a hit of the sixties.
In 1964 Japan opened the bullet train between Tokyo and Osaka, the first high-speed line, famous ever since for being on time.
The same year the SR-71 Blackbird spy plane first flew, at more than three times the speed of sound, records still unbeaten.
Toyota's Corolla arrived in 1966. More than fifty million later, it is the best-selling car name in the world.
The Boeing 737 first flew in 1967 and became the best-selling airliner of the century, the workhorse of short routes.
Then came the jumbo jet. The Boeing 747, with its famous hump, opened up cheap long-distance travel for half a century.
That same year Concorde flew, and would carry passengers across the Atlantic at twice the speed of sound until 2003.
In 1973 Arab producers cut oil supplies. Fuel queues and soaring prices made many countries start saving energy.
In 1981 France's TGV opened between Paris and Lyon, breaking speed records and spreading high-speed rail across Europe.
Europe's Airbus A320 first flew in 1987, the first airliner flown by digital controls, and now one of the most common in the sky.
Ukraine's Antonov Mriya, with six engines, was the heaviest aircraft ever built, until it was destroyed in fighting near Kyiv in 2022.
In 1991 Sony sold the first lithium-ion battery. The same idea would one day power the electric car.
In 1994 the Channel Tunnel joined England and France by rail, the first fixed link since the Ice Age.
In 1997 Toyota launched the Prius, the first mass-produced hybrid, pairing a petrol engine with an electric motor.
China's BYD began with batteries, turned to cars, and by 2024 sold more battery-electric cars than anyone.
The Airbus A380, with two full decks, was the largest passenger airliner ever built, but airlines preferred smaller twins and production ended in 2021.
Tesla's Roadster showed that an electric car could be fast and go far, the first road car on lithium-ion cells.
In India the tiny Tata Nano aimed to move families off scooters, but sold less than hoped.
From 2008 China built high-speed rail at astonishing speed, and now has the largest network in the world.
The Boeing Dreamliner, built largely of carbon fibre, burned far less fuel and opened long routes between smaller cities.
In 2010 the Nissan Leaf became one of the first electric cars made for ordinary buyers.
Airbus answered with the A350, another long-range twin made largely of carbon fibre.
Waymo, born inside Google, now carries paying passengers in several American cities with no one at the wheel.
Tesla's Model 3 pushed electric cars into the mainstream and became the world's best-selling electric car for several years.
After two crashes caused by a flawed control system, the 737 MAX was grounded worldwide.
Tesla's Model Y went further, and in 2023 became the best-selling car of any kind in the world.
And China built an airliner of its own, the Comac C919, which carried its first paying passengers in 2023.
From a balloon over Paris to cars that drive themselves, every journey here made the world a little smaller.
